cards: Inputs, outputs, stores, flows, boundaries and energy. Open systems exchange energy and matter; closed systems exchange energy only. Dynamic equilibrium and positive and negative feedback.
Oceans hold about 97% of water; cryosphere about 2%; groundwater, lakes, soil moisture, atmosphere and biosphere hold the rest.
Evaporation, condensation (dew point, cloud formation), precipitation (orographic, frontal, convectional), cryospheric processes and interception.

Inputs: precipitation. Stores: interception, surface, soil water, groundwater, channel. Flows: infiltration, throughfall, stemflow, percolation, throughflow, groundwater flow, overland flow. Outputs: evapotranspiration and runoff.
P = Q + E ± S (precipitation = runoff + evapotranspiration ± change in storage). Shows water surplus or deficit over a year.
Show discharge after a storm: rising limb, peak discharge, lag time and falling limb. Short lag times come from impermeable rocks, steep slopes and urbanisation.
Human impacts on the water cycle
Deforestation increases runoff and reduces interception; urbanisation increases impermeable surfaces; farming and groundwater abstraction change stores.
Precipitation caught by vegetation before reaching the ground; higher in summer and in coniferous forests.
Infiltration is water soaking into the soil; percolation is water moving down from soil into rock. Infiltration capacity depends on soil type and saturation.
Surface runoff when rainfall exceeds infiltration capacity (Hortonian) or when the ground is saturated.
Combined evaporation from surfaces and transpiration from plants. Higher with temperature, wind and low humidity.
Heavy or prolonged rain, saturated ground, impermeable rock, steep slopes, deforestation and urbanisation.
A long period of below-average precipitation. Meteorological, agricultural and hydrological drought; El Niño influences patterns.
e.g. the River Exe or Eden: show how precipitation, land use and soils affect hydrographs and flooding.
Ice sheets and glaciers store water; melting raises sea levels and changes river regimes.
Lithosphere (sedimentary rocks, fossil fuels) is the largest; also oceans, atmosphere, biosphere and cryosphere (permafrost).
Carbon moves between rocks, oceans and atmosphere over millions of years: weathering, sedimentation and volcanic outgassing.
Carbon exchange through photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition and combustion over days to centuries.
Phytoplankton take in CO2 and sink when they die (biological pump). Cold, dense water absorbs CO2 and sinks at high latitudes (physical pump).
The balance of carbon exchanged between stores. Burning fossil fuels and deforestation have increased atmospheric CO2 from about 280 ppm before industrialisation to over 420 ppm.
Links between water and carbon cycles
Warming increases evaporation; ocean acidity rises as more CO2 dissolves; melting permafrost releases methane, a positive feedback.
e.g. Amazon: huge carbon store with a fast cycle. Deforestation reduces interception and transpiration, increases runoff and releases carbon.
Carbon capture and storage, afforestation, renewable energy, international agreements such as the Paris Agreement.
Photosynthesis moves carbon from the atmosphere into biomass; respiration returns it.
Decomposers release carbon to the atmosphere and soil; slower in cold or waterlogged conditions, forming peat.
Burning biomass and fossil fuels rapidly releases stored carbon into the atmosphere.
Capturing and storing carbon in soils, forests, oceans or geological formations.
Permafrost stores huge amounts of carbon; thawing releases CO2 and methane.
Oceans absorb CO2, forming carbonic acid; lower pH damages coral and shellfish.
Effects of rising carbon on climate
Enhanced greenhouse effect, rising temperatures, changing precipitation and more extreme weather.
Permafrost holds carbon; oil and gas extraction and warming threaten carbon and water stores. Management includes insulated pipelines and buildings on piles.
Stretches of coast in which sediment is largely contained; there are 11 major cells around England and Wales.
Constructive waves (strong swash, low frequency) build beaches. Destructive waves (strong backwash, high frequency) erode.
Hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition, corrosion (solution) and wave quarrying.
Headlands and bays form on discordant coasts. Caves, arches, stacks and stumps form through erosion of weaknesses. Wave-cut platforms form as cliffs retreat.
Waves approach at an angle, carrying sediment up the beach in the swash; backwash takes it straight down, moving sediment along the coast.
Beaches, spits (e.g. Spurn Head), bars, tombolos, salt marshes and sand dunes.
Embryo dunes, fore dunes, yellow dunes, grey dunes, dune slacks and mature dunes, with plant succession (psammosere).
Eustatic change: global change in sea volume. Isostatic change: land rises or falls. Emergent landforms: raised beaches. Submergent: rias and fjords.
Hard engineering: sea walls, groynes, rock armour. Soft engineering: beach nourishment, managed retreat. Shoreline Management Plans and integrated coastal zone management.
One of Europe's fastest-eroding coastlines (about 2 m a year) due to soft boulder clay. Groynes at Mappleton protect the village but increase erosion further south.
The coastal zone from the backshore through the foreshore and nearshore to the offshore zone.
Waves, tides and currents. Fetch and wind speed control wave energy.
Mechanical (freeze-thaw, salt crystallisation), chemical (carbonation of limestone) and biological weathering.
Rockfalls, landslides, slumps and soil creep weaken and shape cliffs.
Concordant coasts have rock bands parallel to the coast (e.g. Lulworth Cove); discordant coasts have alternating rock bands at right angles.
Geos are narrow inlets eroded along joints; blowholes form when a cave roof collapses upwards.
Sea-level rise, more storms and greater erosion threaten coastal communities.
e.g. Bangladesh or the Maldives: vulnerable to sea-level rise and storm surges; management limited by cost.
The Earth's structure, convection currents, ridge push and slab pull. Plate margins: constructive, destructive and conservative.
Lava flows, pyroclastic flows, lahars, tephra, gas eruptions and jökulhlaups. Measured by the VEI.
Earthquakes produce ground shaking, liquefaction, landslides and tsunamis. Measured by the moment magnitude scale and Mercalli scale.
The hazard-response curve showing how quality of life falls during a disaster and recovers through relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction.
A disaster occurs when a hazard affects a vulnerable population.
Form over oceans above 26.5 °C, between 5° and 30° from the equator. Hazards: high winds, storm surges, coastal flooding and landslides.
Need fuel, dry conditions and ignition. Impacts on people and ecosystems; managed by controlled burns and firebreaks.
A place facing several hazards, e.g. the Philippines (typhoons, earthquakes, volcanoes).
Monitoring (seismometers, tiltmeters, gas sensors), land-use planning, building design, warning systems and education.
How people view a hazard depends on wealth, religion, education and experience; ranges from fatalism to adaptation.
e.g. Eyjafjallajökull 2010: ash cloud disrupted air travel across Europe, costing airlines millions; little loss of life in Iceland.
e.g. Haiti 2010: magnitude 7.0, over 200,000 deaths due to poverty and poor buildings. Compare with Christchurch 2011.
e.g. Typhoon Haiyan 2013 in the Philippines: storm surge killed over 6,000 people.
Caused by underwater earthquakes displacing water; e.g. Japan 2011 (Tohoku) caused nuclear disaster at Fukushima.
e.g. Australia 2019-20 bushfires burned millions of hectares and killed billions of animals.
The growing interdependence of economies, cultures and people through trade, investment, technology and migration.
Flows of capital, labour, products and services, and information.
Financial, technological (internet, transport), political (free trade, WTO) and the role of TNCs.
Transnational corporations spread production across countries for lower costs and access to markets, e.g. Apple or Unilever.
Trade agreements and tariffs favour some countries; many LICs depend on primary products with volatile prices.
Rules, norms and institutions such as the UN, WTO, IMF and World Bank that regulate global systems.
Areas beyond national control such as the oceans, atmosphere and Antarctica.
Threats from climate change, fishing, whaling and tourism. Protected by the Antarctic Treaty, CCAMLR and IWC.
Economic growth and development but also inequality, cultural homogenisation and environmental damage.
Promotes free trade by reducing barriers and settling disputes; critics say it favours rich countries.
The IMF provides loans and stability; the World Bank funds development. Structural adjustment conditions have been criticised.
Developed countries export high-value goods; many developing countries export low-value raw materials.
Global brands spread consumer culture; supply chains span many countries.
e.g. smartphones or coffee: production, trade and global value chains.
Countries rely on each other for trade, finance and migration, which brings both opportunities and risks.
Difficulties in governing climate change, migration and the global commons due to national interests.
Place is a location given meaning by people; space is a location without meaning.
Insiders know and feel part of a place; outsiders see it from outside, often more objectively.
Endogenous: inside factors such as location, topography and demographics. Exogenous: outside relationships such as flows of people, money and ideas.
Near places (local) and far places (distant but known through media).
Places are represented in different ways, e.g. in media, art, music, statistics and maps.
Reimaging and regeneration to change a place's identity and attract investment, e.g. tourism-led or sport-led.
Census data, geospatial data, photographs, interviews and art help study places.
Study your local place and a contrasting place to explore how relationships and meanings change.
Shaped by physical and human features, history, culture and the people who live there.
Migration, ageing and gentrification change a place's character and identity.
Deindustrialisation and globalisation change jobs and identity (e.g. former mining towns).
Differences in income, health and education between and within places.
Interviews, questionnaires, photographs, environmental quality surveys and census data.
Growth in the proportion of people living in urban areas, driven by rural-urban migration and natural increase.
Movements of people from cities to suburbs, to rural areas, and back into city centres.
Megacities have over 10 million people. World cities like London have global influence.
Post-industrial cities, mixed-use developments, gated communities and edge cities.
Cities are warmer than surrounding areas because of heat-absorbing surfaces, waste heat and less evapotranspiration.
Impermeable surfaces increase runoff and flood risk. Sustainable urban drainage systems (SUDS) reduce it.
Air pollution from traffic and industry (smog), waste disposal, and environmental problems in growing cities.
Reducing ecological footprint through public transport, green spaces, renewable energy and recycling.
Inequality, deprivation and segregation in cities; regeneration aims to reduce these.
Compare two cities (e.g. London and Mumbai) in terms of growth, inequality and urban policy.
Improving run-down areas through redevelopment, e.g. London Docklands or King's Cross.
Wealthier people move into poorer areas, improving housing but displacing existing residents.
Migration creates diverse cultural areas but can lead to segregation.
Cities have higher temperatures, more rainfall and thunderstorms, poorer air quality and wind tunnels between tall buildings.
Rapid growth leads to informal settlements (slums), e.g. Dharavi in Mumbai.
Landfill, incineration, recycling and reduction strategies; LICs often lack formal systems.
Ecological footprint, green belts, brownfield development and public transport.
Air pollution, water pollution, dereliction and loss of green space.
